item.title: How Did NASA's Asteroid Bennu Samples Reveal Secrets of the Solar System's Birth?
item.description: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are helping scientists piece together how our Solar System first came together 4.5 billion years ago.

item.title: How Did Nuclear Bomb Tests Leave Behind Hidden Clues in Honey, Teeth, and Shark Eyes?
item.description: Decades after nuclear weapons tests stopped, radioactive traces they left behind are still turning up in surprising places — and helping scientists solve puzzles about honey, baby teeth, and the world's longest-living sharks.

item.title: How Did a Simple Daily Pill Show a 70% Lower Dementia Risk for Certain People?
item.description: Scientists studying over 13,000 adults found that a common, inexpensive daily pill was linked to a 70% lower dementia risk — but only for people whose genes give them a particular trait. The surprise? It all comes down to platelets.

item.title: How Did Scientists Recreate the Universe's First 2 Billion Years in a Computer Simulation?
item.description: Scientists have built Lumina, one of the largest cosmic simulations ever, recreating 2 billion years of the early universe and showing how dark matter, gas, and starlight shaped the first galaxies.

item.title: How Did Aging Muscles Trade Strength for Protection?
item.description: As we grow older, our muscles shift from fast-twitch to slow-twitch fibers — and scientists now believe this is not just a sign of decline, but a clever survival strategy that trades power for protection.

item.title: How Did 53 Orangutans Find Safety After Borneo's Devastating Fires?
item.description: When forest fires swept across Borneo this summer, a dedicated rescue team sprang into action — saving 53 orangutans and giving them a second chance in the wild.

item.title: How Did Dunwoody College Students Build a Brand-New Car for a Minneapolis Veteran?
item.description: Dunwoody College of Technology automotive students refurbished a 2020 Hyundai Elantra for a US Navy veteran through the NABC Recycled Rides for Schools program, giving him the freedom to reach doctor's appointments and daily errands.

item.title: Can a Roll of Tape Really Beat Sandbags at Keeping Floodwater Out?
item.description: A UK experiment showed that ordinary rolls of tape can block up to 99% of floodwater sneaking past a door, easily beating the 70% kept out by traditional sandbags — a handy trick for families when a storm surge hits with little warning.

item.title: How Did a Tiny Island Protect Over 20 Percent of Its Ocean Waters?
How Did Mayo Clinic Discover New Ways to Fight Zombie Cells That Drive Aging?
item.description: Scientists at Mayo Clinic have uncovered fresh details about 'zombie' cells — aging cells that linger in the body and fuel inflammation. Seven new studies map how these cells differ, why they harm us, and how everyday compounds like the one in tomatoes might help fight back.

item.title: How Did Jupiter Use Plasma Waves to Build an Invisible Shield Around Itself?
item.description: NASA's Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter defends itself from the solar wind using a clever symphony of plasma waves and multiple shock layers — a system far more intricate than Earth's single-layer shield.

item.title: How Did Jupiter Use an Invisible Shield of Plasma Waves to Deflect the Solar Wind?
item.description: Jupiter's Juno spacecraft discovered the gas giant's bow shock works like a cosmic symphony, using plasma waves with multiple frequencies to deflect the solar wind.

item.title: How Did a High School Senior Prank His Principal on His Birthday — and Change Both Their Lives in the Process?
item.description: A Georgia high school student surprised his principal with a fake school fight for his 51st birthday — but the real story is how they both grew from the experience. One teen learned that people can change, and one principal learned that small acts of kindness ripple further than we imagine.

item.title: How Did the Romans Make a Cup That Changes Color Like Magic?
item.description: The Lycurgus Cup, made by Roman artisans nearly 1,800 years ago, glows green in daylight and flashes red when lit from within. Scientists have only now figured out how the ancient glassmakers pulled off this dazzling trick.

item.title: How Did a Hidden Ocean Chain Reaction Drive Earth's Great Ice Ages?
item.description: New research from the University of St Andrews shows how cooling from massive northern ice sheets may have rippled through the oceans to Antarctica, stirring up a chain reaction that pulled carbon dioxide from the air and tipped the planet into ice age after ice age.

item.title: How Did Tiny Magnetic Vortices Teach Scientists to Watch a Computer Brain Switch States?
item.description: Scientists filmed the tiniest magnetic whirlpools — called skyrmions — rearranging for the first time, opening a path toward computers that think more like our brains while using far less power.

item.title: Where Did These 10 New Animals Get Discovered — in Labs, Airports, and Even a Parking Lot?
item.description: Scientists are finding brand-new animal species in the most ordinary places — inside university labs where they've been studied for years, at airport fuel depots, in cemetery walls, and even in a bundle of moss from an apartment parking lot. A new roundup from Listverse shows that biodiversity can hide right beside us.

item.title: How Did Two Electrons Working Together Break Physics' X-Ray Energy Limit?
item.description: Scientists discovered that when two helium electrons team up during high-harmonic generation, they can produce X-rays far more energetic than a single electron ever could — breaking a decades-old physics rule.

item.title: What Did a Balloon Telescope See in the Sun's Hidden Magnetic Web?
item.description: A balloon-borne solar observatory called Sunrise-III soared 35 kilometers above Earth in 2024 to peer at the Sun's quiet regions. What it found: an intricate magnetic canopy of thread-like structures woven through the solar atmosphere, revealing how our star's hidden magnetic wiring may help heat its outer layers.

item.title: Could Van Gogh's Starry Night Capture a Real July 1889 Sky?
item.description: A new study matches the swirling stars in Van Gogh's famous painting to the actual night sky over Saint-Rémy on July 22, 1889 — and the Hyades cluster in Taurus takes center stage.
